mcqs.question: Why does a status column with only 4 distinct values compress far better than a row containing a customer name, timestamp, and float mixed together?
options: Row-stores never support compression of any kind
Compressing a column of similar, low-cardinality values (dictionary encoding) exploits repetition that a row mixing unrelated data types doesn't have
Compression only works on numeric columns, never on text
The status column is always physically smaller in bytes regardless of compression
mcqs.explanation: Compression algorithms exploit repetition and similarity; a low-cardinality column grouped together is full of it, while a row mixing a name, timestamp, and float has little shared structure to compress. Row-stores can compress too, just less effectively for this reason, and compression isn't limited to numeric data.

mcqs.question: An analyst filters a report to Q1 and Q2, and to only the West and East regions simultaneously. Which OLAP cube operation is this?
options: Roll-up
Drill-down
Dice — selecting a sub-cube by fixing values across multiple dimensions at once
Slice — fixing a single dimension to one value
mcqs.explanation: Dice fixes values or ranges across multiple dimensions simultaneously (time and region here), which is exactly this scenario. Slice fixes only one dimension, and roll-up/drill-down are about moving between levels of a hierarchy, not filtering across dimensions.

mcqs.question: A table is partitioned by order_date. A query filters WHERE order_date >= '2026-07-01'. What does partition pruning do here?
options: It skips reading partitions before that date entirely, without opening those files at all
It decompresses every partition before checking the date filter
It has no effect unless the table is also sorted by amount
It only works if the query also filters on region
mcqs.explanation: Partition pruning skips whole partitions that can't match the filter, based on the partition key — here, entire date partitions before the cutoff are never opened. It doesn't require decompressing first, doesn't depend on an amount sort, and doesn't need an additional region filter to work.

mcqs.question: A team migrates their live application's order-status-update traffic to a column-store database expecting better performance. What's the likely outcome?
options: Performance improves uniformly across all operations
There's no difference since column-stores and row-stores handle all workloads identically
Only read performance is affected; writes remain exactly as fast as before

Point lookups and small frequent updates get slower, since column-stores must reassemble rows from separate column locations and often handle small updates via append-then-compact rather than fast in-place writes
mcqs.explanation: Column-stores are optimized for scan-heavy analytical access, not point lookups or frequent small updates — fetching one row means touching many separate column locations, and updates often go through an append/compaction path rather than fast in-place writes. This is the same OLTP/OLAP mismatch as running analytics on a row-store, just with the failure modes reversed.

mcqs.question: What trade-off does a materialized view make in exchange for faster query response on an expensive, frequently-run aggregation?
options: It requires disabling compression on the underlying fact table
It only works for queries with no WHERE clause
Some staleness — the view reflects data as of its last refresh, though incremental refresh can keep this to seconds or minutes
It eliminates the need for the underlying fact table entirely
mcqs.explanation: A materialized view pre-computes results, so queries against it are fast but potentially slightly stale until the next refresh — incremental refresh keeps that staleness window small. It doesn't require disabling compression, doesn't remove the need for the base fact table, and works fine with filtered queries built on top of it.

mcqs.question: A fact table is partitioned by order_date, but most analytical queries filter by region instead. What's the consequence, and what's the fix?
options: No consequence — partition pruning works regardless of which column is filtered
Queries filtering by region get no benefit from date-based partition pruning and must scan every partition; adding a clustering/sort key on region within partitions can restore pruning-like benefits
The warehouse will automatically re-partition the table by region without any action needed
This means columnar storage provides no benefit at all for this table
mcqs.explanation: Partition pruning only helps when the query filter matches the partition key — a region filter against a date-partitioned table scans everything. Adding a clustering/sort key on region is the practical fix, since automatic re-partitioning isn't something warehouses do unprompted, and columnar layout still helps with column selection even without pruning.
